transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Maya (Nova CTO), Arjun (ML Eng), Hannah (Infra)

Summary (auto): Quick run through of prefix caching strategy, focusing on operational safety for multi-tenant workloads and realistic hit rates based on Nova's customer traffic. Action items and pilot scoping at end.

[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, we'll do a quick intros. I'm Sofia Ramirez, AE at Redwood. With me is Liam, our SE.
[00:12] Maya: Hi Sofia, thanks. Maya here, CTO at Nova, and I have Arjun and Hannah. We, um, really want to understand how prefix caching behaves at scale.
[00:20] Liam: Great. Today we'll walk through our recommended cache key design, common hit-rate profiles, and how we isolate tenants to avoid cross-tenant leakage. We'll also talk latency/throughput tradeoffs and the VPC/on-prem constraints you mentioned.
[00:35] Arjun: Quick ask up front — our workload is ~70% short prompt completions with long tail of longer sessions; does that impact hit rates drastically?
[00:45] Liam: Yes, the distribution matters. Short, repeated prefixes give high hit rates; long session KV cache is different. We'll show examples.

--- Topics: Hit rates and workload patterns ---
[01:10] Liam: For prefix caching we distinguish two caches: static prefix caches (shared precomputed token states for common prompts) and runtime KV caching which is per-session. The prefix cache is where you get big wins on token cost and latency.
[01:30] Maya: Are those prefix keys tenant-scoped? We can't have shared keys across customers.
[01:38] Liam: By default Redwood namespaces prefix keys per-tenant — prefix keys are hashed with tenant id + model id + prompt fingerprint. So multi-tenant safety comes from namespace separation. In hosted mode we also encrypt keys at rest.
[01:55] Hannah: Is that enforced at the KV layer or in the routing layer? We run VPC and want to see network-level guarantees.
[02:04] Liam: It's enforced at the application layer; we use per-tenant namespaces in the cluster and policies at the KV tier. For Dedicated/Private deployments you can opt to have physically separate KV clusters or isolated namespaces.
[02:18] Arjun: Ok that helps. What about collisions from similar prompts? We have many customers using templated prompts where only vars change.
[02:27] Liam: We recommend fingerprinting the canonicalized prompt — strip whitespace, replace variable slots with placeholders, then hash. That increases reuse while keeping safety. Example: "Summarize: [doc]" becomes "summarize:[SLOT]" so you could share the prefix cached partials for the static part.

--- Hit rates & numbers ---
[03:05] Liam: Typical hit rates we observe in production: for templated chat systems you can see 30–60% prefix cache hit rates for initial tokens, sometimes higher for system prompts. For open prompt workloads with high variance, it drops to single-digit percent. Key is to measure against your top-k prefixes.
[03:25] Maya: For Nova our telemetry shows ~18% repeat prefix fraction across daily traffic; is that promising?
[03:32] Liam: Yes, 18% is useful — that can cut per-token compute significantly for those requests. With batching and cache prefetching our internal numbers show 20–40% latency reduction on median and much bigger tail reductions on the cached subset.
[03:48] Arjun: Do you have a model for expected cost savings? We care about TCO.
[03:54] Liam: Conservatively, if 18% of tokens are hit and those saved tokens are early decoding steps, you might see 10–20% reduction in token compute costs. We can run a specific run-rate model if you share traces.

--- Cache key design and TTLs ---
[04:30] Liam: Key format we recommend: H(tenant_id || model_tag || prompt_fingerprint || canonicalization_version). We also include model quantization variant in the key when cache is model-specific. That prevents using a prefix computed on a float16 variant against a quantized runtime.
[04:52] Hannah: So if we update model variants or quantization we have cache invalidation?
[04:58] Liam: Yes, changing model binary or quantization profile bumps the canonicalization_version or model_tag so old cached entries are not used. You can choose soft TTLs or hard invalidation during rollouts.
[05:12] Arjun: For TTL policies, what are typical values?
[05:16] Liam: Depends — system prompts could be long TTLs (days–weeks) if static; user-specific prefixes are shorter (minutes–hours). We often apply LRU with size-based eviction and per-tenant quotas to avoid noisy neighbors.

--- Multi-tenant safety and quotas ---
[05:50] Liam: Important for multi-tenant: per-tenant namespaces + quota controls. We enforce per-tenant cache memory caps and request throttles. If a tenant exceeds their cache quota we evict their least-recently-used entries first.
[06:05] Maya: Can a noisy tenant cause eviction of others if they're in the same cluster?
[06:09] Liam: Only if you choose a shared KV pool without per-tenant quotas. Our managed Dedicated option sets hard quotas per-tenant; in Private you can provision isolated KV or configure namespace limits in the cluster.
[06:22] Hannah: For on-prem, we'd prefer separate KV instances per major customer groups for compliance. Is that supported?
[06:29] Liam: Yes, in Private deployment we can ship a per-tenant KV cluster or a per-customer namespace with enforced OS-level separation. You'll get the runbook for that in the security pack.

--- Eviction strategies & sizing ---
[07:00] Liam: Size the cache based on expected distinct prefixes and average size per cached entry (kv cache stores key + compressed hidden states). Example: a 16k token hidden-state chunk per prefix entry could be X MB — we usually compress and quantize internal activations where possible. For high-volume customers we recommend sharding by tenant hash to distribute hot keys.
[07:30] Arjun: You just said quantize hidden-state — do you quantize activations in cache? Is there fidelity loss?
[07:36] Liam: We support quantized cache entries (8-bit or 4-bit) for certain model families with acceptable fidelity degradation. There's a small accuracy delta — we run regression tests to ensure output quality stays within your SLO. Quantized cache is a tradeoff: smaller memory footprint, slightly higher deserialization compute, minimal quality delta.
[07:57] Maya: Hmm, we'd need to see a quality/regression report.
[08:00] Liam: We'll include synthetic evals plus suggestions to validate on your eval set.

--- Batching & latency tradeoffs ---
[08:25] Liam: Batching improves throughput but can add latency jitter. Prefix cache can reduce the per-request decoding steps which reduces time in the critical path. We combine prefix caching with continuous batching: if a request hits a prefix cache for first N tokens we skip generating those and only batch the remaining tokens.
[08:48] Arjun: Are there SLOs you recommend to keep 99th percentile latency low?
[08:51] Liam: Keep your target per-request queuing delay below X ms; Redwood's runtime can prioritize low-latency lanes and do micro-batching. For your 200ms p50 goal we typically suggest a max batch window < 10ms for latency-sensitive endpoints. For throughput endpoints you can accept larger windows.

--- Faults, fallbacks and safety ---
[09:30] Liam: If cache lookup fails or KV is flaky, Redwood has policy-driven fallbacks: 1) fall back to full decode on same model; 2) fallback to cheaper model variant; 3) return degraded response with notice depending on route policy. You can configure these per-route.
[09:52] Hannah: In VPC mode we have strict egress rules. How do you handle KV lookups if KV is external?
[09:58] Liam: For VPC/Private we can co-locate KV inside your VPC. For hosted we have peering options. We'll need your egress rules for the pilot.

--- Security, encryption, audit ---
[10:30] Maya: A few compliance questions: are prefix cache entries encrypted at rest? Do you log keys?
[10:36] Liam: At-rest encryption with customer-managed KMS is available for Private and Dedicated. For hosted, keys are encrypted with KMS (we can provide SOC2 docs). We don't log raw cached activations; audit logs record lookups as metadata (route, tenant, timestamp) — customers can choose to disable logging of key fingerprints.
[10:58] Maya: Good. RBAC and admin controls?
[11:02] Liam: RBAC integrates with your SSO; you can restrict who can purge caches or bump canonicalization versions.

--- Pilot scoping and benchmarks ---
[11:30] Liam: For the pilot we propose: 1) share your top-100 prefixes and a 48h sample of traffic (anonymized), 2) Redwood runs offline hit-rate simulation, 3) run live pilot on Nova dev cluster for 2 weeks with monitoring and hit-rate dashboards, 4) joint eval on quality regressed due to quantized cache.
[11:52] Arjun: Timeline?
[11:54] Sofia: If we get data by Friday, Liam can run the sim next week and we can start pilot the week of 3/16.
[12:00] Maya: Works for us.

--- Q&A / clarifications ---
[12:10] Arjun: A couple technical Qs — how is the cache sharded and do you do consistent hashing?
[12:15] Liam: We use consistent hashing for sharding hot keys; key -> vnode -> shard. That reduces movement on reshard. For tenant isolation we prefer tenant-aware sharding so tenants map to fixed shard ranges when required.
[12:30] Hannah: What about memory reclamation during GC spikes?
[12:34] Liam: We monitor heap and do pro-active eviction based on LRU + size thresholds; for worst-case spikes we can reprovision or failover to separate shards.

--- Closing recap ---
[12:50] Sofia: Recap: we'll send docs and security pack, run sim, scope pilot. Action items noted. Thanks everyone.
[13:05] Maya: Thanks, really helpful.
[13:08] Hannah: bye

References & links mentioned: prefix-caching-best-practices (link sent after call), security-whitepaper (SOC2/KMS), benchmark-spreadsheet (to be shared), pilot runbook (dev cluster steps).

End of transcript.
